prompt: Lesson 1's `GET /v1/books/1` names a book and lets the method say what to do with it. What does a gRPC request name?
hint: Think of `Reserve`.

choices.text: A procedure on a service
choices.why: Right. The request is a call: the service, the method, and a message of arguments.

choices.text: A resource, by its address
choices.why: That is REST, the style of lesson 1.

choices.text: The fields the client wants back in this answer
choices.why: That is GraphQL, lesson 3.

choices.text: An operation inside an XML envelope described by a WSDL
choices.why: That is SOAP, lesson 5.

prompt: Older RPC systems tried to make a remote call look exactly like a local one. What went wrong with that?
hint: Ask what a local call cannot do.

choices.text: Their binary formats could not be read by a person debugging them
choices.why: gRPC is binary too, and that is a cost, not the failure the section names.

choices.text: A function call cannot carry more than one argument across a network
choices.why: A message carries as many fields as it needs.

choices.text: Local calls were too slow to imitate
choices.why: The opposite: a local call is fast and dependable, and pretending a remote one is like it is the problem.

choices.text: The network failed in ways their code had no plan for
choices.why: Right. A remote call fails halfway, runs slow or loses its answer; gRPC builds deadlines and status codes into every call for this reason.

prompt: Which of these are true of gRPC and not of lesson 1's REST API? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at the last two rows of the comparison table.

choices.text: It runs on HTTP/2 and nothing else
choices.why: Right. `curl` in HTTP/1.1 could not even read the answer.

choices.text: The client chooses a path and a method for each request
choices.why: That is REST. A gRPC client calls a generated function, and the path is the library's business.

choices.text: The contract file is required, and both sides are generated from it
choices.why: Right. In lesson 1 the contract is optional, and lesson 6 writes one.

choices.text: Its errors carry HTTP status codes such as 404
choices.why: A failed gRPC call still answers HTTP 200; its own code comes in the trailers.

choices.text: What travels cannot be read without the schema
choices.why: Right. `--decode_raw` showed numbers where the names should be.

prompt: In `int32 copies = 3;`, what identifies the field in the bytes that are sent?
hint: Only one of the parts ever leaves the program.

choices.text: The name `copies`
choices.why: Names stay in the `.proto` and the generated code; that is the JSON habit.

choices.text: Its position in the message, counting from the top of the block
choices.why: Fields can be written in any order; position means nothing on the wire.

choices.text: The type and the name together
choices.why: The tag carries a wire type, not `int32`, and never the name.

choices.text: The number 3, packed into the tag
choices.why: Right. The tag packs the number 3 with the wire type.

prompt: Why is the zero value of `Availability` called `AVAILABILITY_UNSPECIFIED` and not `IN_STOCK`?
hint: What does a reader see when the field was never set?

choices.text: A field never set reads as zero, and that should not look like good news
choices.why: Right. A missing value would otherwise read as `IN_STOCK`.

choices.text: proto3 forbids a real state from using the number zero
choices.why: It only requires the first value to be zero; what you call it is the design choice.

choices.text: The compiler sorts values by name, so the zero one must start with A
choices.why: Values keep the numbers you give them; nothing is sorted.

choices.text: Zero is kept for errors in every enum, so a real state needs another number
choices.why: Zero is the default, not an error; errors are status codes.

prompt: In a `.proto` file, the word put in front of a field's type to make it a list is ___.
hint: `RestockSummary` has one.

prompt: Field numbers from 1 up to which number fit in a one-byte tag?
hint: The next one needs two bytes.

prompt: A tag byte is `1a`, which is `00011010` in binary. What field number does it carry?
hint: Drop the last three bits.

prompt: `od` shows a string field as `12 0c 44 6f 6d …`. What does the `0c` tell the reader?
hint: `12` is the tag, and its wire type is 2.

choices.text: That this is field number 12
choices.why: The field number is in the tag, `12`, which is field 2.

choices.text: How many bytes of the value follow: twelve
choices.why: Right. Wire type 2 is a length and then that many bytes, here `Dom Casmurro`.

choices.text: The value itself, the varint 12
choices.why: That reading belongs to wire type 0, as in `18 0c` for the copies.

choices.text: Which text encoding the bytes of the string are in
choices.why: A `string` is always UTF-8, so nothing on the wire says so.

prompt: `copies: 300` was encoded as `18 ac 02`. Which number do the varint bytes `96 01` encode?
hint: `96` is `10010110`. The second byte is worth 128 times its value.

prompt: What does `protoc --decode_raw` print for Dom Casmurro's `availability`?
hint: Raw means with no `.proto`.

choices.text: `availability: IN_STOCK`
choices.why: That is `--decode`, which has the schema to name both.

choices.text: `4: IN_STOCK`
choices.why: The value's name comes from the schema as much as the field's does.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since enums are dropped when the schema is missing
choices.why: Nothing is dropped; the number is all the bytes ever held.
Right. Field 4, value 1: the bytes hold numbers and nothing else.

prompt: Which generated name does `stock_client.py` use to make its calls?
hint: The client's side of the service.

choices.text: `StockServicer`
choices.why: That is the class the server inherits and fills in.

choices.text: `StockStub`
choices.why: Right. One method per `rpc`, and calling one sends the call.

choices.text: `add_StockServicer_to_server`
choices.why: That connects the server's class to a running server.

choices.text: `StockLevel`
choices.why: A message, which the stub returns; it makes no calls.

prompt: Somebody fixes a bug by editing `stock_pb2_grpc.py` by hand. Next week `stock.proto` changes. What becomes of the fix?
hint: How are the generated files made again?

choices.text: `protoc` refuses to run until the edit is undone
choices.why: It never looks at the old file.

choices.text: It is kept, since `protoc` only adds what is new
choices.why: The file is written whole every time.

choices.text: It is gone, written over by the next generation without a word
choices.why: Right. Generated files are never edited; the fix belongs in the `.proto` or in your own code.

choices.text: Python refuses to import a generated file that was edited
choices.why: Python cannot tell; it imports whatever is there.

prompt: How does the server's `Reserve` stop two reservations that arrive together from both taking the last copy?
hint: Look at the `WHERE` of its `UPDATE`.

choices.text: The check and the subtraction are a single `UPDATE` with `stock >= ?`
choices.why: Right. The database changes the row for one of them, and the other sees no row changed.

choices.text: gRPC runs one call of each method at a time
choices.why: There are eight worker threads, and two calls of one method can run together.

choices.text: The interceptor queues calls that come from the same till
choices.why: It only prints the method and the metadata.

choices.text: `context.abort` locks the row until the call ends
choices.why: `abort` ends a call with a status; it locks nothing.

prompt: Put one `GetStock` call in order, from the client's command to its output.
hint: The interceptor sees a call before its method does.
items: The stub encodes the message and sends it to `/shelf.stock.v1.Stock/GetStock`
The interceptor prints the method and the `x-till` entry
`GetStock` reads the row and returns a `StockLevel`
trap: The server's log line appears before the method runs, not after.

prompt: Match each `rpc` line to its kind of call.
hint: Look for the word `stream` and which side it is on.
right_distractors: two calls, one in each direction

prompt: The watch printed three levels and then `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`. How many calls did the client make to `WatchStock`?
hint: A stream is not a series of requests.

choices.text: Three, one for each level
choices.why: That is polling. The server sent each level on the call that was already open.

choices.text: Two: one to open the stream and one to close it
choices.why: The deadline closed it; nothing was sent to close it.

choices.text: One
choices.why: Right. One call, three messages, one status.

choices.text: Four: three levels and a fourth for the status
choices.why: The status ends the same call that carried the levels.

prompt: A till must send 2,000 scanned barcodes and get back one total once all have arrived. Which kind of call fits?
hint: Who sends many messages, and who sends one?

choices.text: Server streaming
choices.why: That has one request and many answers, the other way round.

choices.text: Bidirectional, because both sides send something
choices.why: Both do send, but the server sends once, at the end; nothing needs to run both ways.

choices.text: A unary call per barcode
choices.why: Two thousand calls, and no single answer that needs all of them.

choices.text: Client streaming, the shape of `Restock`
choices.why: Right. Many messages in, one out, once the client has sent the last.

prompt: A till asks to reserve 5 copies of a book that has 2. Which status fits?
hint: Would the same request be fine on another day?

choices.text: `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, because five is too many
choices.why: Five is a valid request; it fails only because of what is on the shelf now.

choices.text: `FAILED_PRECONDITION`
choices.why: Right. The request is fine and the system is not in a state to accept it.

choices.text: `NOT_FOUND`, since five copies cannot be found
choices.why: The book exists; `NOT_FOUND` is for an ISBN that names nothing.

choices.text: `UNAVAILABLE`
choices.why: The server answered; `UNAVAILABLE` is for a service that could not be reached.

prompt: Which of these failures is worth sending again, unchanged, after a pause?
hint: Which one says nothing about the request itself?

choices.text: `NOT_FOUND` for an ISBN
choices.why: The same question about the same data gets the same answer.

choices.text: `INVALID_ARGUMENT` for zero copies
choices.why: The same mistake sent again fails again.

choices.text: `UNAVAILABLE` after the connection was refused
choices.why: Right. The request never reached a server, so trying later can work.

choices.text: `UNIMPLEMENTED` for an unknown method
choices.why: The method will not appear because you waited.

prompt: A `Reserve` call ends with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`. What does the till know about the copies?
hint: The deadline is when the client stopped waiting.

choices.text: Nothing for certain: the copies could be gone already
choices.why: Right. The server could have taken them just before the deadline, and only asking again, with `GetStock`, tells which.

choices.text: They were not taken, because the call failed
choices.why: The call failed for the client; the work may already have been done.

choices.text: They were taken, because a server always finishes what it starts
choices.why: The server sees the call cancelled and may stop before the `UPDATE`.

choices.text: They were taken and then put back by gRPC
choices.why: gRPC knows nothing about the database; nothing is undone for you.

prompt: Facts about a call rather than about its message, such as `x-till: till-1` or a credential, travel in the call's ___.
hint: The interceptor read them from `invocation_metadata`.

prompt: Which change to `StockLevel` leaves the bytes an old client receives exactly as they were?
hint: Which half of a field ever reaches the wire?

choices.text: Keeping the name `copies` and moving it to number 6
choices.why: On the wire that is field 3 removed and a new field 6 added.

choices.text: Changing `copies` from `int32` to `string`
choices.why: The wire type changes, and an old reader misreads it.

choices.text: Renaming `copies` to `count` and keeping number 3
choices.why: Right. The name never travels; only code and JSON that used it notice.

choices.text: Removing `copies` and reserving its number
choices.why: Compatible, but an old client now reads zero copies for every book.

prompt: An old till, built with the first `stock.proto`, reads a level from the next release, which removed `title` and added `location = 5`. What does it see?
hint: The capture decoded exactly this.

choices.text: An error, because the message holds a field it does not know
choices.why: Unknown fields are skipped or kept, never an error.

choices.text: The location printed where the title should be
choices.why: That happens only if `location` reuses number 2, which `reserved` prevents.

choices.text: The title it last saw, kept from the previous answer
choices.why: Each message is read on its own; nothing is carried over.

choices.text: An empty title, and field 5 kept as an unknown field
choices.why: Right. Removing a field is compatible on the wire and still a change a screen can show.

prompt: To stop field number 2 from ever being used again in a message, you write `___ 2;` inside it.
hint: `protoc` then refuses a file that uses it.

prompt: Put the parts of one unary gRPC call in the order they cross the connection.
hint: The result comes last.
items: Request data: `00`, a four-byte length, the `BookRef`
trap: `:status: 200` is not the call's result; `grpc-status` is, and it comes after the body.

prompt: A call to a method the warehouse does not have came back as `HTTP/2 200`. Where is the failure?
hint: Look past the empty line.

choices.text: Nowhere: 200 means it worked
choices.why: 200 says the HTTP exchange worked, nothing about the call.

choices.text: In the body, as a JSON object with an `error` field
choices.why: That was lesson 1's API; gRPC sends no JSON.

choices.text: In the trailers: `grpc-status: 12`
choices.why: Right. 12 is `UNIMPLEMENTED`, with `Method not found!` beside it.

choices.text: In the status line, which a gRPC client reads as 501
choices.why: The status line said 200, and the client reads the trailers instead.

prompt: Why can a web page's JavaScript not call the warehouse directly?
hint: Where does a gRPC call put its result?

choices.text: `fetch()` cannot read the trailers
choices.why: Right. The status of every call arrives there, and gRPC-Web moves it into the body for that reason.

choices.text: Browsers do not speak HTTP/2
choices.why: They do; what a page cannot do is control the framing or read trailers.

choices.text: Browsers refuse a binary body in a `POST`
choices.why: A page can send bytes; uploads do it all the time.

choices.text: Port 50051 is blocked by browsers
choices.why: Nothing about the port matters here.

prompt: A gRPC request body begins `00 00 00 01 2c`. How long is the message that follows?
hint: The first byte is the flag; the next four are one number, in hexadecimal.

prompt: The bookshop wants partners to read its catalogue, mostly from scripts and browsers, and wants HTTP caches to take the load. What fits?
hint: Who is on the other end, and what can a cache keep?

choices.text: gRPC, because its messages are smaller
choices.why: Smaller does not help a browser that cannot call it, or a cache that keeps no `POST`.

choices.text: REST with JSON, as lesson 1 built it, and `GET` for every read
choices.why: Right. Strangers, `curl`, browsers and `GET` caching are its home ground.

choices.text: gRPC with a server stream for every read
choices.why: Streams solve changing data, not strangers with browsers.

choices.text: gRPC behind a cache that keeps `POST` answers
choices.why: HTTP caches do not keep `POST` answers, and every gRPC call is one.

prompt: Match each situation to what fits it.
hint: Two of them put something in front of a gRPC service.

pairs.left: Ten services of your own, in four languages
A public catalogue that caches should serve
A web page that must call a gRPC service
Partners who want plain JSON from a gRPC service

prompt: A colleague wants to move the warehouse to REST with JSON, saying it is the same thing. What would the tills lose? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of the watch, the `.proto` and the timeout.

choices.text: Status codes of any kind
choices.why: REST has its own, the HTTP codes of lesson 1.

choices.text: One open call that pushes each change as it happens
choices.why: Right. REST would poll, or need a second technology beside it.

choices.text: A contract the compiler holds both sides to
choices.why: Right. In REST the contract is optional and checked only if somebody writes it, as in lesson 6.

choices.text: The ability to run over HTTP
choices.why: Both run over HTTP; gRPC needs HTTP/2 in particular.

choices.text: A deadline that travels with each call to the server
choices.why: Right. Over REST the server learns nothing of how long the client will wait.

prompt: `curl` shows `HTTP/2 200` for a `GetStock` call, then the trailer `grpc-status: 5`. What should a till do?
hint: Find code 5 in the table of codes.

choices.text: Treat it as a success, since HTTP said 200
choices.why: 200 only says the exchange worked; the call's result is the trailer.

choices.text: Retry after a pause, since 5 is a passing failure
choices.why: The passing one is 14, `UNAVAILABLE`.

choices.text: Tell the till the ISBN is unknown, and not retry
choices.why: Right. 5 is `NOT_FOUND`, and asking again gets the same answer.

choices.text: Generate the stub again, since 5 means the method is missing
choices.why: A missing method is 12, `UNIMPLEMENTED`.

prompt: The next release removed `title` WITHOUT a `reserved` line, and a year later somebody gives the free number 2 to a new `string location`. Old tills still run. What happens?
hint: Nothing here stops the file from compiling.

choices.text: `protoc` refuses the file
choices.why: It would, with `reserved 2;`, which is exactly what is missing.

choices.text: Old tills fail on an unknown field
choices.why: Field 2 is not unknown to them; they know it as `title`.

choices.text: Old tills skip field 2, since its name in the new file changed
choices.why: Names do not travel, so nothing tells them it changed.

choices.text: Old tills show the location as the title, with no error
choices.why: Right. A string in field 2 is exactly what they expect, so they read it as the title.
